name: The G.'s Spot
subtitle: A barbershop. Findable, reportedly, by those who know where it is.
description:
Nobody can give you directions to this place. Four people have tried, all of them sincerely, all of them describing a different corner, and every one of them got here today without difficulty. There is a demographic in Silvora Reefs that finds it without looking, and Wino-T's explanation is that they grew up around those parts, which he delivers on the beat and which is the whole of the explanation you are going to get.

Inside: modest from the street, and then not. Two chairs, a long counter, a wall of bottles in colours that were discontinued, and a hallway to the back that is signposted for a lavatory and has, on three occasions, delivered guests into what they later described as a completely different business.

And the mirrors. There is a great deal of mirror in a barbershop. In this one, that is a decision somebody made.
revisit:
Wino-T does not look up from the fade he is working and says your name on the beat, the way he says everything, and the clippers do not miss a stroke doing it.

Sir Jerry is at the far chair with a towel over his forearm and the unhurried bearing of a man who has never once been late for anything because he has never once conceded that a thing could start without him. The third mirror holds the room, and holds the back of a head at a desk, and holds Monsieur Albert in an excellent coat with an expression of the most enormous patience.

There is a cup on the shelf by the third mirror. It is full. It was full yesterday.

lucid.2: Under the clippers there is a rhythm that the clippers are matching rather than making.
lucid.3: The clippers stop for the length of a word, and the rhythm underneath does not, and then the clippers catch up.
lucid.4: Nothing in this room makes its own noise. Every sound in here is keeping time with something in another room.

ambient: Sir Jerry sharpens a razor in nine strokes and says 'Nine, as the physicians had it, and they were wrong about a great deal but not about nine' — to nobody in particular, and to the razor, and possibly to the profession itself.
Something moves in the dark at the back of the shop with more shoulder in it than the space behind those chairs can account for, and settles, and is courteous about having moved at all.
A woman comes in off a street that is not outside the door, hangs her coat on a hook that has been empty all evening, and takes the near chair without anybody having to tell her it was free.
The clippers change pitch as they go over the crown and Wino-T's sentence changes with them, and the sentence was already going to rhyme, and the rhyme lands on the pitch change.
In the third mirror, the man at the desk reaches for something outside the frame. In the room, nothing reaches for anything.

objects.name: the mirrors
objects.description:
Three on the long wall, one behind each chair, and a fourth at the end of the room that faces the third — so the room goes off into itself in a corridor of diminishing Olivers, each one slightly greener than the last.

They do not all agree, and the disagreement is not the ordinary disagreement of angles.

The near one has you in the chair, which is correct. The far one has the room from above and slightly behind, from a position about nine feet up and on the other side of a wall that has no other side — which is not an angle any mirror in this building could take, and is not an angle at all so much as a *viewpoint*.

And the third has been showing the same thing for a fortnight, on and off, at no schedule anybody has isolated. Wino-T covered it for two days and then stopped, because a sheet over a mirror is a question mark and a mirror is not, and nobody in the history of barbering has ever asked a barber about a mirror.

It shows a man at a desk. From behind. Working.
objects.repeat: He has not turned round. In a fortnight of coming in here at every hour this shop keeps, he has not once turned round, and the back of that head has become as familiar to you as a face.

lucid.2: The shoulders in the mirror move in a rhythm. Small, repetitive, two-handed.
lucid.3: It is not a rhythm. It is typing, and there are pauses in it, and the pauses are where the choices go.
lucid.4: He has your shoulders. He has the specific set of them that you have been told about by two tailors and one physiotherapist, and he is using them to do something you are not doing.

objects.monocle: Through the gold the third mirror gives up the pretence of being a mirror and becomes a window, and the room on the other side is nine feet by eleven with a green-shaded lamp and a door on two trestles, and the man at the desk is wearing green with purple accents, and he does not turn round.

passive.text: The far mirror's angle is from above and behind — from a corner of the ceiling on the other side of a wall that has no corner in it and no other side. That is not a reflection, whatever else it is. Nothing in this room is standing where that view is being taken from.

Four mirrors, four accounts of one room, and no two of them consistent with each other. That is not an optical problem; optics are boringly reliable and would give you four wrong answers that agreed. Four accounts that disagree is not a fault in the glass. It is a disagreement about what the room *is*.

clue.title: A man at a desk, from behind
clue.text: One of the G.'s Spot mirrors has shown the same image for a fortnight: a man at a desk, seen from behind, working, who has never once turned round.

clue.title: Green with purple accents
clue.text: Under the monocle the mirror becomes a window onto a small room with a green-shaded lamp and a door on two trestles. The man at the desk wears green with purple accents — Oliver's colours, inverted. He does not turn round.

check.prompt: Stop looking at what is in the mirrors and let the mirrors look at you for a minute. Four glasses, four accounts of one room, and one of them is not an account of this room at all.
check.success:
The first two are glass and behave. The third is not glass and is not behaving and has not been, for some time, and it has been extremely patient about being the only one anybody notices.

It is not showing a room. It is *holding* one — the way a man holds a door for somebody who is taking a long while to arrive — and it has been holding it since before the barber was knighted.
check.failure: Three mirrors, and the third one goes on being slightly wrong in a way that stays exactly at the edge of what can be said about it, and the harder you attend to it the more ordinary it becomes, which is itself the point and is no use to you.

clue.title: The third mirror is holding a door
clue.text: The third mirror at The G.'s Spot is not reflecting a room but holding one open, and has been doing it for a very long time.

objects.name: the hallway to the back
objects.description:
Signposted, in a small brass plaque with a small brass arrow, and the plaque is the only entirely unambiguous object in this building — it says what it means, it points where it points, and it has never once done anything else.

Three customers on record have gone down it and come out somewhere else.

One in a chandlery, on a street that has not had a chandlery on it in sixty years. One in a room full of filing cabinets and no windows and nobody in it. And one — and this is the one Wino-T tells, on the beat, when the shop is full and the telling will land — came out in the Möbius Strip Club at eleven o'clock at night, having gone for a wash at four in the afternoon, and was entirely calm about the whole business, and did not go back for his coat.

All three returned. Every one of them, within the day, by the front door.

None of them can describe the return. Not evasively — they try, and they are willing, and there is simply nothing there to describe.
objects.repeat: The brass arrow points the same way it has always pointed. It is the only thing in this building that has never once disagreed with itself, and you have started using it as a control.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the hallway is four feet long and ends in a door, and behind the door is a lavatory, and it is a perfectly ordinary lavatory with a cracked cistern. The other places are not down the hallway. They are down the *account* of the hallway, and the account is longer than the hallway and always has been.

check.prompt: Walk down it and count. Keep counting on the way back, and do not let the count become a thing you are performing rather than a thing you are doing, because this building can tell the difference.
check.success:
Four paces to the door. You go in, you come out, you count four paces back, and you are in the barbershop, and Wino-T is on the same bar of the same hum.

And the count in your head has kept going past four. It is at nineteen. You stopped walking at four and the count went to nineteen and you were not walking for fifteen of them, and you were somewhere, and there was a room, and it had filing in it.
check.failure:
Four paces to the door, and a lavatory with a cracked cistern, and four paces back, and Wino-T on the same bar of the same hum. Nothing. A hallway did a hallway's job.

Except that the count in your head is at nineteen and you cannot make it be at eight.

clue.title: Fifteen paces unaccounted for
clue.text: Four paces down the hallway, four back, and a count that reached nineteen. Fifteen paces occurred in which no walking was done, and there was a room, and it had filing in it.

objects.name: the before-and-afters
objects.description:
Sir Jerry's wall. Forty-odd pairs, pinned in a grid that has been kept square over what must be decades, each pair a customer before and the same customer after, and every pair signed by the customer underneath with a comment they were evidently invited to write and took seriously.

The comments are extraordinary, and they are extraordinary in the same direction. *Didn't know myself.* *My own mother walked past me in the street.* *A new man, and the old one is not missed.* One of them, in a hand that is shaking badly enough to be legible as shaking, says only *thank you*, twice, the second time underlined.

And the photographs show a haircut.

In every single pair — forty-odd of them, across decades, different men, different decades of fashion — the difference between the before and the after is about an inch and a half off the sides. That is all. That is the entire visible intervention, and it is the same intervention every time, and forty men have looked at the result and written down that they were not the same person.
objects.repeat: You go along the grid again, looking for one pair where the before and the after are the same man and the difference is the inch and a half. You have done this four times now and you find the same thing every time, which is that they are the same man, and that they are not.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the photographs are unchanged and the *comments* are not. Every comment is in the same hand. Forty-odd customers, forty-odd signatures, one hand — and it is a hand that has been trying, on each occasion, to look like somebody else's, and getting better at it as the wall goes on.

passive.text: They are not lying and they are not deluded. Read the comments under the pairs: every one of them is written by a man who came in unhappy and went out having been told he was a new man, and believed it, and was right — and the photographs are of the same head with an inch and a half off it.

'A new man, and the old one is not missed.' That is not a satisfied customer's phrasing. That is a formula. Forty-odd variations on one sentence, in forty-odd hands, none of them copying the others, all of them arriving at the same construction.

clue.title: An inch and a half off the sides
clue.text: Forty customers describe being transfigured by Sir Jerry's haircuts. The photographs, in every case, show an inch and a half off the sides.

clue.title: Forty signatures, one hand
clue.text: Under the monocle every customer comment on Sir Jerry's wall is in the same handwriting — a hand attempting, each time, to look like somebody else's, and improving as the wall goes on.

check.prompt: There is a photograph on this wall with you in it. Not a resemblance and not a coincidence — you, in a pair, before and after. Look for it without letting Sir Jerry see what you are looking for.
check.success:
Level voice, hands where they were, weight unchanged. You take the whole wall in as a wall, and you take the eleventh photograph from the left in as one photograph among many, and you ask him about the frames.

He talks about frames. And while he talks you get the rest of it: the date on the print, the other two men in it, and the fact that in this photograph you are laughing at something the man on your left has just said, and the man on your left is not in the parish and never has been.
check.failure:
It is the eleventh from the left and it has you in it and your face does the arithmetic before you have authorised the arithmetic.

He sees it. He does not say anything about it, which is worse, and he moves down the bar to give you the room, which is worse than that.

clue.title: The man on your left
clue.text: A photograph on the wall of The G.'s Spot shows you laughing at something said by a man who has never been in the parish.

objects.name: the shape at the back of the shop
objects.description:
Monsieur Albert does not come forward. Monsieur Albert has never come forward, in forty years, and the not-coming-forward has the quality of an arrangement rather than an inability.

He occupies the dark past the last chair the way a bookcase occupies a corner — settled, permanent, taking up a defined volume — and he is an owlbear, and he is a nobleman, and both of those things are simply true in this shop and neither of them requires anything from you except that you not make a performance of noticing.

He is visible in the third mirror: a great deal of shoulder in an excellent coat, feathers at the collar going to fur at the cuff, an expression of the most enormous patience.

He is not visible in the room. You have checked this in both directions, twice, looking from the glass to the air and back — and on the second attempt he inclined his head at the checking, from the mirror, courteously, acknowledging it, while the corresponding volume of air by the last chair went on containing precisely nothing.
objects.repeat: Still only in the glass. Still courteous about it. Still positioned exactly where a person would stand if they wanted to be in the room without being in the way of anybody's work.
objects.monocle: Through the gold, Monsieur Albert is in the room. Solidly, warmly, taking up a great deal of it, in an excellent coat. It is the *room* that has been declining to include him, and the monocle overrules the room, and he looks back at you with an expression that has waited a long time to be looked at directly.

passive.text: He has been in this shop longer than the shop has been in this street, and nobody has spoken to him in forty years, and he is not bitter about it. That is the part that is hard to be in the room with. He has made his peace with a thing that should not be survivable and he has made it courteously.

clue.title: The room is what omits him
clue.text: Under the monocle Monsieur Albert is solidly present in the barbershop. It is not that he is absent — it is that the room has been declining to include him, and the lens overrules the room.

check.prompt: There is an owlbear in the mirror and he is being extremely courteous about forty years of not being spoken to. Look at him. Directly, in the glass, and do not look away when he notices.
check.success:
You keep it level. You do not stare and you do not perform not-staring, and you ask him how long he has been at this establishment as though asking a barman about his shift.

He answers, delighted, at length, and the answer contains the following: forty years, no reflection of his own on this side, and the fact that nobody has addressed him directly since a Thursday he can name.
check.failure:
You get as far as the address and then some part of the arrangement gets through — the depth of him, the fact that he is *in* the glass rather than reflected by it — and your face does what a face does.

He looks away first, to spare you, which is the worst thing that has happened tonight.

clue.title: Nobody has addressed him since Thursday
clue.text: Monsieur Albert has been in the third mirror for forty years and can name the last Thursday anybody spoke directly to him.

objects.name: the wall of bottles
objects.description:
Hair tonics, every one of them discontinued, in colours that were discontinued along with them: a green that is not manufactured any more and has not been since before the war, an amber with no modern equivalent at all, and a purple down at the end which Wino-T says was never made in the first place and came with the shop when he bought it.

The labels are in a typeface you know.

You know it the way you know a voice through a wall — before the words, before the recognition, in the part of the mind that files things without asking. You have gone up close to it four separate times over the fortnight, and it has been four different typefaces, and every one of them has been the one you know.

The amber bottle is the one to watch. Nobody in this shop touches it, and the level in it is lower than it was on Tuesday.
objects.repeat: Fifth time, fifth face, and all of them the one you know. The amber bottle has not been touched by anybody in this shop in the fortnight you have been watching it, and the level in it is lower than it was.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the labels are not printed. They are struck — one character at a time, with the uneven pressure of a machine being worked by somebody who does not touch-type, and the purple bottle's label has been struck twice over itself because the first attempt came out as ONIONS.

passive.text: The amber one is forty per cent something. It is labelled as a hair tonic and it was discontinued before either of us was born and the level in it is going down, and nobody in this shop drinks it, and Wino-T pours himself something at the end of the night that does not come out of any bottle on this shelf.

clue.title: The label came out as ONIONS
clue.text: Under the monocle the tonic labels are struck one character at a time by an uneven hand. The purple bottle's has been struck twice over itself, because the first attempt came out as ONIONS.

check.prompt: The back shelf holds something with no label, in a bottle nobody in this shop reaches for, at a level that goes down anyway. Have what the shop has when the shop is not being watched.
check.success:
It is clear and it is cold and it tastes like the first line of something.

And for the length of one swallow every name behind the bar is legible at once — not the labels, the *names*, the ones the bottles have rather than the ones they were given — and all of them are versions of the same name, declined like a noun in a language with cases.
check.failure:
It is clear and it is cold and it is extremely strong, and it goes down and stays down and does nothing else whatsoever.

No memory, no kitchen, no afternoon belonging to somebody else. Just alcohol, doing the one job alcohol does — and the owner watches you find that out from the other end of the bar, on the beat, with an expression that is not quite sympathy.

clue.title: One name, declined
clue.text: Under the unlabelled bottle, every name behind the bar at The G.'s Spot resolves into versions of a single name, declined like a noun.

objects.name: the third mirror, gone to a doorway
objects.description:
The frame is still a frame. That is the strange part and it stays strange: the wood is the wood, the spots in the silvering are exactly where the spots have always been, the whole apparatus is precisely the mirror it was on Tuesday and will presumably be the mirror it is tomorrow.

What is in it is no longer an image of a room.

It is the room. At the correct size, with the correct amount of air in it, and the boards on the far side run continuous with the boards under your feet — same width, same grain, meeting at the frame without a join, the way one floor meets itself across a doorway.

The lamp is on over there. The chair is pushed back.

And Monsieur Albert is standing next to it, in an excellent coat, in the room, solidly, casting a shadow, for the first time in forty years. He is not going through and he has not been asked to and he would not accept the invitation. He has waited forty years to be *somewhere*, and he is going to be there, and he would rather like that noticed by somebody before the evening ends.
objects.monocle:
Nothing.

The lens has nothing to say. You turn it over, you breathe on it, you hold it at the angle that has worked all fortnight — and the room through the gold is the room, at the same size, with the same door in it.

Albert, in the room, solidly, notices you notice that. "Quite," he says. "It has run out of hidden. There is only the thing now, monsieur, and the thing is a door, and I find I have nothing whatever to add to it after forty years of having a great deal to add to everything."
objects.repeat: Still open. It is not going to close on its own, and that is not the same thing as it being patient, and you have now stood in front of it on three separate evenings doing arithmetic you already know the answer to.

passive.text: Every deduction you have made in a fortnight terminates here. There is nothing further to be worked out from this side of it — no reading of the evidence that does not require walking through — and that has been true since before you admitted it.

Four inches of nothing, and a floor on the other side that will take a man's weight; you can see the boards and the grain in the boards and a nail head somebody countersunk badly. The body has already worked out the step. The body is not the part that is hesitating.

check.prompt:
Go through. Nothing is stopping you and nothing has been stopping you for some time, and that is the part that will need thinking about afterwards, on the other side, if there is an afterwards and if there is a side.

There is no way back through a seam. Whatever is unfinished in Silvora Reefs stays unfinished.
check.success:
You go through.

There is no membrane and no cold and no drama, and the last thing behind you is somebody not saying anything, and then you are standing on boards in a room nine feet by eleven with a green-shaded lamp in it.
check.failure:
Your foot goes over the edge and your weight does not follow it, and you stand for a while in a doorway with one leg committed, which is not a dignified way to arrive anywhere and is a completely honest description of the last fortnight.

Then the knee that has been going since the harbour makes the decision for you, and you go through badly, and land on boards, in a room nine feet by eleven, with a green-shaded lamp in it.

exits.hang_hi: a walk you will not be able to describe afterwards, ending at a floor that hangs from nothing
exits.mobius: down toward the water and the light that is nearly red
exits.lishush_mush: round the corner, into a smell like a chord being held
